title: Taylor & Maclaurin series
examples: How do I find the first few terms of a Taylor series?
What does the error bound tell me about my approximation?
Is the Maclaurin series just a special case of Taylor series?

explain.say: Today we will learn about series approximations. We will build these series step by step. Think of it like building with mathematical blocks.
The Taylor polynomial uses derivatives at a point. You need the function and the point x equals a. We use the formula involving factorials.
For the Maclaurin series, the point a is always zero. This simplifies the formula greatly for us. The first few terms are easy to find.
The error bound helps us check how good our approximation is. We use the remainder term, Rn, to estimate the error. This gives us confidence in our answer.

items: Taylor series uses derivatives at point 'a'

faq.q: What is the difference between Taylor and Maclaurin series?
faq.a: A Maclaurin series is simply a Taylor series where you choose the point a to be zero. It is a specific case of the general Taylor formula. You can think of it as a special shortcut.
asks: Is Maclaurin just Taylor at zero?
When do I use Maclaurin instead of Taylor?

faq.q: Why do I need to find the error bound?
faq.a: The error bound tells you the maximum possible error in your approximation. It lets you know how close your calculated value is to the true value. It is a measure of accuracy.
asks: What does the remainder term mean?
How accurate is my approximation without the error bound?

faq.q: How many terms should I use for the approximation?
faq.a: You should use enough terms until the error bound is smaller than the required precision. If you need three decimal places, make the error bound less than zero point zero zero five. Always check the required accuracy.
asks: Should I stop when the term is very small?
Is there a rule for choosing 'n'?

faq.q: Does the function need to be differentiable for this to work?
faq.a: Yes, the function must be sufficiently differentiable at the point a. This means its derivatives up to a certain order must exist. If the derivatives are complicated, the series might not converge.
asks: What if the function is not smooth?
Do all functions have a Taylor series?

faq.q: What are the steps for building the series?
faq.a: First, find the first few derivatives of the function. Second, evaluate these derivatives at the point a. Third, plug everything into the general Taylor formula. Finally, simplify the resulting polynomial.
asks: What is the process for finding the series?
Can you walk me through the steps again?

facts: The Taylor polynomial approximates a function using its derivatives at a point.
The Maclaurin series is the Taylor series centered at zero.
The error bound uses the maximum value of the derivative on the interval.
The general formula involves factorials of the term number.

quiz.say: If we approximate f(x) using the first two terms, what does the error bound estimate?
quiz.show: Error bound estimates the maximum error.

options.show: The value of the function at zero.
options.say: The value of the function at zero.

options.show: The maximum possible error in the approximation.
options.say: The maximum possible error in the approximation.

options.show: The actual value of the function at x.
options.say: The actual value of the function at x.

options.show: The value of the third derivative.
options.say: The value of the third derivative.

quiz.why: The error bound is specifically designed to give you the maximum possible size of the error.

wrong.0: This is only relevant if the center point a is zero.
wrong.2: This is the value you are trying to find, not the error.
wrong.3: The error bound uses the next higher derivative, not just one specific derivative.

quiz.say: For the Maclaurin series of e^x, what is the coefficient of the x squared term?
quiz.show: Coefficient of x^2 in e^x series.
quiz.why: The general term for e^x is one divided by n factorial, so for n=2, it is one divided by two factorial.

wrong.0: This confuses the power of x with the coefficient.
wrong.1: This would be the coefficient for the x to the first power.
wrong.2: This incorrectly uses the power of x in the denominator.

quiz.say: If the interval is from one to two, what must the error bound use for M?

options.show: The maximum value of the derivative on [1, 2].
options.say: The maximum value of the derivative on [1, 2].

options.show: The value of the derivative at two.
options.say: The value of the derivative at two.

options.show: The value of the derivative at one.
options.say: The value of the derivative at one.

options.show: The value of the derivative at the midpoint.
options.say: The value of the derivative at the midpoint.

quiz.why: The constant M must be the largest value of the derivative's absolute value over the entire given interval.

wrong.1: You must check the whole interval, not just the endpoint.
wrong.2: Checking only the starting point is not enough for the whole interval.
wrong.3: The maximum value might occur at the endpoints, not necessarily the middle.
